records.source: Πάλιν οὖν αὐτοῖς ἐλάλησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς λέγων· Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου· ὁ ἀκολουθῶν ἐμοὶ οὐ μὴ περιπατήσῃ ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ, ἀλλ’ ἕξει τὸ φῶς τῆς ζωῆς.
records.gloss: Again therefore to them spoke the Jesus saying, "I am the light of the world; the [one] following me not not will walk in the darkness, but will have the light of the life."

L.12: So again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world; the one who follows {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} will certainly not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life."

R.12: Jesus spoke to the people again. He said, "I am the light of the world. People who follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} will never walk in the dark. They will have the light that gives life."

decisions.choice: again, so: Jesus speaks once more to the crowd at the Festival of Tabernacles, taking up the scene of 7:37-52
alternatives: a new occasion, unconnected to the feast
decisions.reason: The words point back to Jesus's public teaching at the feast (7:14, 28, 37). The disputed story of 7:53-8:11 now stands between, but it was not part of the earliest copies of John (see the note at 7:53), and without it 8:12 follows straight on from 7:52: the Pharisees have just dismissed Jesus, and he speaks again in the temple (8:20). "Them" are the people gathered there, with Pharisees among them (8:13).

decisions.choice: I am the light of the world: the second of John's sayings "I am" with a picture; the world here is all humanity
decisions.reason: With a predicate, "I am" is ordinary grammar, as in 6:35; the "I" is written out and emphatic. The saying takes up the prologue, where the Word is the light of humanity, the true light coming into the world (1:4-9), and it returns at 9:5 before Jesus gives sight to a man born blind. The world here is humanity as a whole, all people living in the dark without God, not one nation only (compare 3:19; 12:46).

decisions.choice: light at the feast: the lamps of Tabernacles, the pillar of fire, and the light God promised in Isaiah
decisions.reason: The saying is spoken at the Festival of Tabernacles, in the temple near the treasury (8:20). Later Jewish tradition (Mishnah Sukkah 5:2-4) describes great lamps lit in the temple courts during the feast, so bright that they lit up Jerusalem; John does not mention them, so the link is likely but not certain. The feast recalled Israel's years in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42-43), when God went before the people in a pillar of fire to give them light (Exodus 13:21), and Israel followed. Isaiah promises that the people who walk in darkness will see a great light (Isaiah 9:2) and that God's servant will be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6).

decisions.choice: will certainly not walk in the darkness; the light of life: the light that gives life
decisions.reason: The double negative is the strongest way to say "not" in Greek. To walk is to live one's life, and the darkness is the world without God, as in 1:5 and 12:35, 46. In "the light of life" the genitive describes what the light gives: life, as the bread of life is the bread that gives life (6:35); the light also belongs to life itself, since the Word's life was the light (1:4).

decisions.choice: the people; the light that gives life
alternatives: them; the light of life (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable names who "them" are (meaning decision m1) and states the sense of "the light of life" (meaning decision m4). Literal and Balanced keep the familiar phrase, which is the plain translation.

decisions.choice: Those who follow (B), People who follow (R) ... never
decisions.reason: The Greek "the one following" means anyone at all; a plural keeps that sense without a he or she. "Never" carries the emphatic negative (meaning decision m4), as in 6:35.

records.heading: The light of the world

records.source: εἶπον οὖν αὐτῷ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι· Σὺ περὶ σεαυτοῦ μαρτυρεῖς· ἡ μαρτυρία σου οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθής.
records.gloss: Said therefore to him the Pharisees, "You about yourself testify; the testimony of you not is true."

L.13: So the Pharisees said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You are testifying about {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}; {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} testimony is not true."

R.13: The Pharisees said to Jesus, "You are the only witness speaking about {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}. So {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} testimony does not count as true."

decisions.choice: true: valid as evidence, able to stand in a court
alternatives: true as opposed to false: a charge that Jesus is lying
decisions.reason: The Pharisees speak in the terms of the law, which lets a matter stand only on the evidence of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). A claim about oneself, with no one else to support it, does not count as proof. They are not saying that Jesus lies but that his word alone proves nothing.

decisions.choice: the Pharisees use Jesus's own words against him
decisions.reason: In 5:31 Jesus himself granted the rule: "If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true." The Pharisees now apply it to his claim to be the light of the world (8:12). Jesus answers in 8:14-18, as he did in 5:32-37, by naming the Father as the second witness.

decisions.choice: You about yourself: the emphasis falls on Jesus as the one speaking about himself
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is written out and stands first, and "about yourself" comes before the verb. The stress is on who is giving the evidence.

decisions.choice: on your own behalf (B); the only witness ... does not count as true (R)
decisions.reason: The same wording as 5:31, where Jesus states the rule the Pharisees now quote, so that readers can hear the echo. Readable spells out the legal point (meaning decision m1).

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Κἂν ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ, ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία μου, ὅτι οἶδα πόθεν ἦλθον καὶ ποῦ ὑπάγω· ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ οἴδατε πόθεν ἔρχομαι ἢ ποῦ ὑπάγω.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to them, "Even if I testify about myself, true is the testimony of me, because I know from where I came and where I go; you but not know from where I come or where I go.

L.14: Jesus answered and said to them, "Even if I testify about {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going; but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.

R.14: Jesus answered, "Even if I am a witness speaking about {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} testimony is true. I know where I came from, and I know where I am going. But you do not know where I come from or where I am going.

decisions.choice: true: truthful, a reliable account of the facts
decisions.reason: In 5:31 Jesus said that testimony about himself is "not true", meaning that it does not stand as evidence on its own. Here he makes a different point: whether or not it meets the rule of evidence, what he says about himself is true, because he alone knows the facts, where he came from and where he is going. No other human witness can speak to that. He then grants the legal rule again and meets it by naming the Father as his second witness (8:17-18). The two sayings do not contradict each other: one is about what counts as evidence, the other about whether he speaks the truth.

decisions.choice: where I came from and where I am going: from the Father, and back to the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus has come from God and is returning to the one who sent him (7:28-29, 33; 13:3; 16:28). His opponents think they know where he comes from, Galilee and Nazareth (7:27, 41, 52), and do not understand where he is going (7:35-36); 8:21-22 returns to it.

decisions.choice: I came ... I come: the past tense points to his coming into the world, the present to where he comes from
decisions.reason: In the first half Jesus looks back on the one act of coming from the Father; in the second the present tense speaks of his origin in general, which is what they do not know. "Where I go" is present in form with a future sense: where he is going.

decisions.choice: on my own behalf
decisions.reason: The same words as 5:31 and 8:13, so the legal language stays visible.

decisions.choice: have no idea
decisions.reason: Gives the sharp contrast of the emphatic "you" with Jesus's "I know".

records.source: ὑμεῖς κατὰ τὴν σάρκα κρίνετε, ἐγὼ οὐ κρίνω οὐδένα.
records.gloss: You according to the flesh judge, I not judge no one.

L.15: You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.

R.15: You judge people by human standards, only by what you can see. I am not judging anyone.

decisions.choice: according to the flesh: by merely human standards, by outward appearance
alternatives: you judge by my flesh, that is, by my human appearance
decisions.reason: "Flesh" here is human nature in its limits, seeing only the outside. Jesus has already told them not to judge by appearances (7:24); compare 1 Samuel 16:7, where the LORD looks on the heart. Their judgment of him rests on where he seems to come from (7:27, 41-42, 52).

decisions.choice: I judge no one: Jesus does not judge in the way they do, and judging is not the purpose of his coming
decisions.reason: The Father has given all judgment to the Son (5:22, 27), and Jesus will speak of his judgment in the next verse and in 8:26. But he did not come to condemn the world (3:17; 12:47), and he does not pass judgment on mere appearances as they do. The next verse qualifies the statement: when he does judge, his judgment is true.

decisions.choice: you ... I: a sharp contrast
decisions.reason: Both pronouns are written out and set against each other. Greek also allows the double negative, "not ... no one", for a single strong "no one".

decisions.choice: by human standards (B); by human standards, only by what you can see (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom (meaning decision m1); Literal keeps "according to the flesh".

records.source: καὶ ἐὰν κρίνω δὲ ἐγώ, ἡ κρίσις ἡ ἐμὴ ἀληθινή ἐστιν, ὅτι μόνος οὐκ εἰμί, ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ.
records.gloss: And if judge but I, the judgment the mine true is, because alone not I am, but I and the [one] having sent me Father.

L.16: But even if I do judge, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} judgment is true, because I am not alone, but [it is] I and the Father who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.16: But even if I do judge, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} judgment is true. I am not alone when I judge. The Father who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: the Father who sent me: the SBLGNT reads "Father"
decisions.reason: A few manuscripts lack the word "Father" and read "the one who sent me"; among them are the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae. Most manuscripts, including the early papyri, have it, and 8:18 has the same phrase with "Father". The sense is the same either way, since "the one who sent me" always means the Father in John. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: true: genuine, sound, judgment that is what judgment ought to be
decisions.reason: Here John uses a different adjective from the one in 8:13-14 and 8:17. It means real or genuine, as in "the true light" (1:9) and "the true bread" (6:32). Jesus's judgment is the real thing, not a human verdict by appearances (8:15); in 5:30 he called it just, because he seeks the will of the one who sent him.

decisions.choice: even if I do judge: a concession that qualifies 8:15
decisions.reason: The "I" is written out at the end of the clause for weight. Jesus does not take back "I judge no one"; he adds that, when he does judge, he does not judge alone.

decisions.choice: not alone: the Father is with the Son in all he does
decisions.reason: Jesus does nothing on his own (5:19, 30); the one who sent him is with him and has not left him alone (8:29; 16:32). This prepares the two-witness argument of 8:17-18.

decisions.choice: [it is]
decisions.reason: English needs a verb after "but"; the Greek leaves it out.

decisions.choice: in it: it is I together with (B); is with me (R)
alternatives: but I and the Father who sent me (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out what "I and the Father" means here: the Father judges together with him (meaning decision m4).

records.source: καὶ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ δὲ τῷ ὑμετέρῳ γέγραπται ὅτι δύο ἀνθρώπων ἡ μαρτυρία ἀληθής ἐστιν.
records.gloss: And in the law but the your it has been written that of two people the testimony true is.

L.17: And in your law it is written that the testimony of two {{gender:people|men}} is true.

R.17: Your own law says that when two {{gender:people|men}} give the same testimony, it counts as true.

decisions.choice: the rule of two witnesses in the law of Moses
decisions.reason: The law requires two or three witnesses before a person is convicted (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; compare Numbers 35:30). Jesus gives the sense of the rule, not the words of one verse.

decisions.choice: your law: the law you yourselves hold to and appeal to
alternatives: a law Jesus treats as belonging to them and not to himself
decisions.reason: The possessive is emphatic. Jesus argues from the authority his hearers accept: on their own terms, his testimony stands. He is not setting himself apart from the law of Moses, which he says testifies about him (5:39, 46); he speaks the same way in 10:34, and in 15:25 of "their law". The phrase does mark the distance between Jesus and those who use the law against him.

decisions.choice: two people: two human witnesses; true: valid as evidence
decisions.reason: The word means human beings, without regard to sex. The argument moves from the lesser to the greater: if the word of two human beings stands in court, how much more the testimony of the Son and the Father (8:18). "True" has the legal sense of 8:13.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The witnesses the law speaks of are human beings in general, so the inclusive word is the default and "men" the traditional alternative.

decisions.choice: your own law
decisions.reason: "Own" carries the weight of the emphatic possessive (meaning decision m2). Readable adds "give the same testimony" to make clear that the two witnesses agree.

records.source: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ καὶ μαρτυρεῖ περὶ ἐμοῦ ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ.
records.gloss: I am the [one] testifying about myself, and testifies about me the [one] having sent me Father."

L.18: I am the one who testifies about {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, and the Father who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} testifies about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

R.18: I am one witness, and I testify about {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}. The Father who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is the other witness, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} testifies about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} too."

decisions.choice: I am the one who testifies: "I am" with a predicate, ordinary grammar
decisions.reason: The participle is the predicate: Jesus names himself as one of the two witnesses. This is not the absolute "I am" of 8:24, 28 and 58.

decisions.choice: the Father is the second witness
decisions.reason: The two witnesses the law asks for are Jesus and the Father (compare 5:32, 37). The Father testifies through the works he gives the Son to do (5:36; 10:25) and through the Scriptures (5:39). The force of the argument lies in who the second witness is: if they knew the Father, they would accept his testimony (8:19).

decisions.choice: I am one who testifies
alternatives: I am the one who testifies (Literal)
decisions.reason: The point is that Jesus is one of two witnesses; "one who" makes that clear in English without losing the emphatic "I am".

decisions.choice: one witness ... the other witness
decisions.reason: Readable names the two witnesses the law requires (meaning decision m2).

records.source: ἔλεγον οὖν αὐτῷ· Ποῦ ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ σου;
records.gloss: Were saying therefore to him, "Where is the father of you?"

L.19: So they were saying to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Where is {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} father?"

R.19: Then the Pharisees asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Where is {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} father?"

decisions.choice: Where is your father?: they take Jesus to mean a human father and ask where this second witness is
alternatives: a question about God, asked in mockery
decisions.reason: A witness had to appear in person. The Pharisees understand Jesus to be speaking of a man and ask him to produce him. The question may also carry a hint about Jesus's birth, as 8:41 may ("We were not born of sexual immorality"), but the text does not say so here.

decisions.choice: they were saying: the Pharisees of 8:13
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject; the Pharisees are the last speakers named. The tense may describe what they kept saying, or simply that they spoke.

decisions.choice: father, lowercase
decisions.reason: The speakers are not thinking of God (meaning decision m1), so "father" is not capitalised in their mouth; in Jesus's answer it is. "Your" takes the setting for pronouns addressed to Jesus.

decisions.choice: the Pharisees
decisions.reason: Readable names the speakers (meaning decision m2).

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς· Οὔτε ἐμὲ οἴδατε οὔτε τὸν πατέρα μου· εἰ ἐμὲ ᾔδειτε, καὶ τὸν πατέρα μου ἂν ᾔδειτε.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus, "Neither me you know nor the Father of me; if me you had known, also the Father of me you would have known."

L.19: Jesus answered, "You know neither {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} nor {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father; if you knew {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, you would know {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father also."

R.19: Jesus answered, "You do not know {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you do not know {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father. If you knew {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, you would know {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father too."

decisions.choice: to know the Son is to know the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus answers that his Father is God, whom they do not know (7:28). The Son makes the Father known (1:18); whoever sees him sees the one who sent him (12:45), and he says the same to his disciples in 14:7-9. Their failure to know Jesus shows that they do not know God.

decisions.choice: if you knew me, you would know: a condition contrary to fact, in the present
alternatives: if you had known me (a past condition)
decisions.reason: The verb "know" has a past form with a present meaning, so the condition speaks about now: they do not know him, and so they do not know the Father.

decisions.choice: my Father, capitalised
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of God, in contrast to the human father the Pharisees had in mind (8:19, first sentence).

records.source: ταῦτα τὰ ῥήματα ἐλάλησεν ἐν τῷ γαζοφυλακίῳ διδάσκων ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ· καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐπίασεν αὐτόν, ὅτι οὔπω ἐληλύθει ἡ ὥρα αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: These the words he spoke in the treasury teaching in the temple; and no one seized him, because not yet had come the hour of him.

L.20: These words {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spoke in the treasury, while teaching in the temple; and no one seized {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, because {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hour had not yet come.

R.20: Jesus said these things while {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was teaching in the temple courts, near the boxes where people put their offerings. But no one arrested {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, because {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} time had not come yet.

decisions.choice: the treasury: the part of the temple courts where the chests for offerings stood
alternatives: a storeroom for the temple's treasure
decisions.reason: Mark 12:41-44 and Luke 21:1-4 tell of people putting money into the treasury, which was a place where anyone could come. Later Jewish tradition (Mishnah Shekalim 6:5) speaks of thirteen collection chests in the temple. The word can also mean a treasure room, but Jesus is teaching in public, so the area by the offering chests is meant, and "in" may mean "at" or "near".

decisions.choice: the temple: the whole temple area with its courts
decisions.reason: This word means the temple courts where people gathered and teachers taught (7:14, 28), not the sanctuary.

decisions.choice: no one seized him because his hour had not yet come
decisions.reason: John says again what he said at 7:30: no one can arrest Jesus before the time the Father has set for his death and glorification (2:4; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). He was speaking openly in one of the busiest places in the temple, and still no one could take him.

decisions.choice: treasury area, temple courts, arrested (B); near the boxes where people put their offerings, time (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable describe the place (meaning decisions m1 and m2) and use "arrested" as in 7:30 and 7:32. Readable says "time" for the appointed hour, as the book's terms allow and as at 7:30.

records.source: Εἶπεν οὖν πάλιν αὐτοῖς· Ἐγὼ ὑπάγω καὶ ζητήσετέ με, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ὑμῶν ἀποθανεῖσθε· ὅπου ἐγὼ ὑπάγω ὑμεῖς οὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν.
records.gloss: Said therefore again to them, "I go away and you will seek me, and in the sin of you you will die; where I go you not are able to come."

L.21: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them again, "I go away, and you will seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you will die in your sin. Where I go, you cannot come."

R.21: Then Jesus spoke to them again. "I am going away," {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said. "You will look for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you will die still guilty of your sin. You are not able to come where I am going."

decisions.choice: I go away: his departure to the Father through his death
decisions.reason: As in 7:33, this verb is John's word for Jesus's return to the one who sent him (13:3; 16:5). He has said where he goes (8:14); his hearers do not know (8:22).

decisions.choice: die in your sin: die with the sin still on you, unforgiven
decisions.reason: To die in one's sin is a phrase from the Scriptures for dying under the guilt of sin, with nothing done to remove it (Ezekiel 3:18-20; 18:24). The point is not the cause of death but the state in which they die: cut off from the one who takes away the sin of the world (1:29).

decisions.choice: sin, singular: the one sin of refusing him
alternatives: a collective word for all their sins
decisions.reason: Here Jesus says "sin"; in 8:24 he says "sins" twice. The singular most likely names the root sin of unbelief, which 16:9 calls sin ("because they do not believe in me") and which leaves all other sins in place (3:18, 36; 9:41). The plural in 8:24 then names the sins that unbelief leaves unforgiven. The singular may also be simply collective; the sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: you will seek me: too late, and not to find life
decisions.reason: In 7:34 Jesus said they would seek him and not find him. Here he says what that means: they will look for him when he is gone and die in their sin. He says to his disciples that they too cannot come where he goes (13:33), but promises to come back and take them to himself (13:36; 14:3); to these hearers he makes no such promise.

decisions.choice: going away, search for (B); look for, still guilty of your sin (R)
alternatives: go away, seek, die in your sin (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the same words as in 7:33-34 so the echo stays visible, and put "where I am going" after the verb, as there. Readable explains the phrase "die in your sin" (meaning decision m2).

records.heading: Where I am going

records.source: ἔλεγον οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Μήτι ἀποκτενεῖ ἑαυτὸν ὅτι λέγει· Ὅπου ἐγὼ ὑπάγω ὑμεῖς οὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν;
records.gloss: Were saying therefore the Jews, "Not will he kill himself, that he says, 'Where I go you not are able to come'?"

L.22: So the Jews were saying, "He will not kill {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, will {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, since {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'Where I go, you cannot come'?"

R.22: The Jewish leaders said, "Surely {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is not going to kill {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}! Is that why {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'You are not able to come where I am going'?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the hostile hearers in the temple, the authorities and those siding with them
alternatives: the listeners in the temple generally
decisions.reason: The scene goes on from 8:13-20, where Jesus answers the Pharisees in the temple treasury, and from 7:35, where "the Jews" took his words about going away in the same mocking way. The speakers are those who reject him and seek his death (7:1; 8:37, 40). John does not say they are only officials; others in the temple who sided with them may be included. It is not the people as a whole: many who hear him believe (8:30), and Jesus himself is a Jew.

decisions.choice: a question that expects no, while raising the thought in mockery
decisions.reason: The question opens with a negative particle that looks for "no" but leaves the idea hanging: "He will not kill himself, will he?" The same particle introduces the Samaritan woman's hesitant question in 4:29. Here the tone is scornful: if no one can follow him, perhaps he means to go where no decent person goes.

decisions.choice: irony: he will indeed give up his life, but not as they mean
decisions.reason: In 7:35 they guessed he would go to the Greeks; now they guess he will take his own life, which was held to be a grave wrong. Again they speak more truly than they know: he will lay down his life of his own accord (10:17-18), though it is they who will put him to death (8:28, 37), and his death is the way he goes to the Father.

decisions.choice: since he says: the reason they offer for their guess
decisions.reason: The word that joins the two parts gives the ground for their question: they reason from his words, "Where I go, you cannot come", which they repeat as he said them in 8:21.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities and those with them, Balanced and Readable name them, as at 7:35 (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: Surely ... not ...? Is that why (B); Surely ... not ...! (R)
decisions.reason: English shows that "no" is expected (meaning decision m2) with "surely ... not", and splits the long question in two. The words they quote are given as each level gave them in 8:21.

records.source: καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τῶν κάτω ἐστέ, ἐγὼ ἐκ τῶν ἄνω εἰμί· ὑμεῖς ἐκ τούτου τοῦ κόσμου ἐστέ, ἐγὼ οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου.
records.gloss: And he was saying to them, "You from the [things] below are, I from the [things] above am; you of this the world are, I not am of the world this.

L.23: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying to them, "You are from the [places] below; I am from the [places] above. You are of this world; I am not of this world.

R.23: Jesus told them, "You come from down here below. I come from heaven above. You come from this world. I do not come from this world.

decisions.choice: below and above: the earthly realm and the realm of God
decisions.reason: The two words name where one comes from: the earth, or heaven where God is. John the Baptist made the same contrast in 3:31 ("the one who comes from above is above all"), and Jesus told Nicodemus that he came down from heaven (3:13). "Below" does not mean the world of the dead; it is this world, as the second half of the verse says.

decisions.choice: this world: human life organized apart from God and set against him
decisions.reason: Key term. John uses "world" for the creation (1:10a), for humanity whom God loves (3:16), and for humanity that refuses God (7:7; 15:18-19). "This world" here is the last: the order to which his hearers belong in their unbelief. Jesus says the same of his disciples later, that they are not of the world as he is not (15:19; 17:14, 16), so the point is not birthplace but where a person's life comes from.

decisions.choice: from ... of: where one comes from, and so what one is
decisions.reason: The same preposition is used in all four clauses. It gives origin, and in John origin shapes character: what is born of the flesh is flesh (3:6), the one from the earth speaks of the earth (3:31). Because they belong to this world, they cannot come where he goes (8:21).

decisions.choice: from the [places] below/above (L); come from (B, R); down here, heaven (R)
alternatives: You are from below; I am from above
decisions.reason: The Greek has "from the [things] below"; Literal brackets "places" so the article stays visible. Balanced and Readable use "come from" in all four clauses, since the point is origin (meaning decision m3). Readable says where "above" is, heaven, as in 3:13 and 3:31, and says "down here" for below.

records.source: εἶπον οὖν ὑμῖν ὅτι ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν· ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι, ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: I said therefore to you that you will die in the sins of you; if for not you believe that I am, you will die in the sins of you."

L.24: So I said to you that you will die in your sins; for if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins."

R.24: That is why I told you that you will die still guilty of your sins. If you do not believe that I am, you will die still guilty of your sins."

decisions.choice: I am: the words with which God names himself, said by Jesus of himself; the claim includes being the one from above whom the Father sent
alternatives: a plain "I am he": I am the one I claim to be (the one from above, the Christ)
the divine name alone, with no thought of his claims in the context
decisions.reason: Jesus says "I am" with nothing after it, and his hearers at once ask, "Who are you?" (8:25), so no predicate is plain from the context, as it is in 4:26 (the Messiah) and 6:20 (it is I). The words are those God uses of himself in the Greek of Isaiah: "that you may know and believe ... that I am" (Isaiah 43:10; also 43:25; 45:18; 46:4), echoing "I am who I am" (Exodus 3:14) and "See now that I, I am he" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Isaiah 43:10 joins knowing and believing to these words as 8:24 and 8:28 do. In the same speech Jesus says he is from above (8:23), and 8:58 ends with "before Abraham was, I am". So the echo of God's name is uppermost, with the claim to be the one from above held within it. Some take it more plainly as "I am he", the one I say I am; that reading is given in the footnote. Marked uncertain because both senses are present and the weight between them is a judgment.

decisions.choice: your sins, plural: the sins left unforgiven
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats what he said in 8:21, but now with the plural. Unbelief, the one sin of 8:21 (meaning decision m3 there), leaves all their sins in place; only the one who takes away the sin of the world can remove them (1:29).

decisions.choice: for if you do not believe: the condition that explains the warning
decisions.reason: "For" gives the reason for the warning just repeated. The warning is not final: it holds unless they believe. Believing is the way out of dying in sin, as eternal life is promised to the one who believes (3:16, 36; 5:24).

decisions.choice: that I am, with no "he" supplied (also in 8:28)
alternatives: that I am who I claim to be
decisions.reason: Because the echo of God's name is uppermost (meaning decision m1), every level keeps the bare words, here and in 8:28, as 8:58 will. Supplying "he" would settle the sense on the plain reading. The English reads as unfinished, as the Greek did to those who heard it (8:25). The footnote gives "that I am he".

decisions.choice: die still guilty of your sins
decisions.reason: As in 8:21, Readable explains the phrase "die in your sins".

records.source: ἔλεγον οὖν αὐτῷ· Σὺ τίς εἶ;
records.gloss: Were saying therefore to him, "You, who are you?"

L.25: So they were saying to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You, who are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"

decisions.choice: an emphatic "you": a challenge
decisions.reason: The question puts "you" first for emphasis: "You, who are you?" After the bare "I am" of 8:24 they demand that he say plainly who he claims to be. The same question was put to John the Baptist (1:19), and in 10:24 they will demand, "If you are the Christ, tell us plainly."

decisions.choice: they: the same hearers as in 8:22
decisions.reason: The subject is not named. The speakers are those Jesus has just been addressing, the ones called "the Jews" in 8:22 (meaning decision m1 there).

decisions.choice: Just who are you? (B); Who are you, then? (R)
decisions.reason: English cannot easily put "you" first twice; Balanced shows the challenge with "just", Readable with "then" (meaning decision m1).

records.source: εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅ τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν;
records.gloss: Said to them the Jesus, "The beginning, what even I speak to you?

L.25: Jesus said to them, "Why do I even speak to you at all?

R.25: Jesus answered them, "Why do I even talk to you at all?

decisions.choice: a question: "Why do I even speak to you at all?"
alternatives: "What I have been telling you from the beginning" (a statement)
"I am what I have told you from the beginning"
"I am, first of all, what I am telling you"
decisions.reason: One of the hardest sentences in John. The SBLGNT prints it as a question, and this translation follows that. Read so, the opening words have a sense they often have in Greek, "at all", and the next word asks "why": Jesus declines to answer again a question his whole speech has answered, and goes on in 8:26 to say he has much more to say and judge. The early manuscripts had no punctuation, so a statement is also possible: the opening words can mean "from the beginning", and the next word "what", giving "what I have been telling you from the beginning" (compare 8:24, 28; 10:25). That reading gives a direct answer to "Who are you?", but it uses the opening words in a sense they rarely have without a preposition. Marked uncertain; the footnote gives the other readings.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text, without added words
alternatives: "I told you at the beginning what I am also telling you" (an early papyrus)
decisions.reason: One early papyrus of John adds "I told you" at the start, which makes the sentence a statement about what Jesus said at the beginning. The other manuscripts do not have it, and it looks like an attempt to make a hard sentence easier. A reviewer should check this note against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: talking (B); answered, talk (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the everyday verb, keeping "even" and "at all" so the question keeps its weariness. Readable says "answered", since he is replying to their question.

records.source: πολλὰ ἔχω περὶ ὑμῶν λαλεῖν καὶ κρίνειν· ἀλλ’ ὁ πέμψας με ἀληθής ἐστιν, κἀγὼ ἃ ἤκουσα παρ’ αὐτοῦ ταῦτα λαλῶ εἰς τὸν κόσμον.
records.gloss: Many things I have concerning you to speak and to judge; but the [one] having sent me true is, and I, the things which I heard from him, these things I speak into the world.

L.26: I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you; but the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is true, and I, what I heard from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, these things I speak to the world."

R.26: There are many things I could say about you and many things I could judge. But the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is real and true. I tell the world the things I have heard from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: I have many things to say and judge: much that he could say against them
alternatives: I must say and judge many things
decisions.reason: "I have ... to say" means there is much he could say, and the pairing with "judge" shows it would be against them. He has authority to judge (5:22, 27), though he did not come to condemn (3:17; 8:15-16).

decisions.choice: but: he holds back and speaks only what the Father gives
decisions.reason: The "but" turns from what he could say about them to what he does say: not his own verdict, but the message of the one who sent him. Even so, his words carry judgment, because they are the true words of God (8:16; 12:48-49).

decisions.choice: true: truthful and reliable
decisions.reason: As in 3:33 and 7:28, the word means that the one who sent him speaks truly and can be relied on. What Jesus passes on is therefore true as well (8:14, 40).

decisions.choice: to the world: to humanity, openly
decisions.reason: Key term. He speaks what he heard into the world, to people at large, not in secret (18:20). The world here is humanity, the people God loves and to whom he sent his Son (3:16-17), not the hostile order of 8:23.

decisions.choice: I tell the world what I have heard (B, R); real and true, could (R)
alternatives: what I heard from him, these things I speak to the world (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the object after the verb, the usual English order. Readable says "could" to show these are things he holds back (meaning decision m1), and "real and true" as at 7:28.

records.source: οὐκ ἔγνωσαν ὅτι τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῖς ἔλεγεν.
records.gloss: Not they knew that the Father to them he was speaking.

L.27: They did not know that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking to them [of] the Father.

R.27: They did not understand that Jesus was talking to them about God the Father.

decisions.choice: did not know: did not grasp, failed to recognize
decisions.reason: The verb means know or recognize. They heard him speak of "the one who sent me" (8:26) but did not grasp that he meant God the Father, though he had named the Father plainly in 8:18-19. The narrator's remark shows how deep their failure to understand goes (8:19, 43).

decisions.choice: the Father: the one he was speaking about
decisions.reason: "The Father" is the object of "was speaking" in the sense "speaking of": he was telling them about the Father. The tense describes what he had been doing all along.

decisions.choice: understand (B, R); Jesus, God the Father (R)
decisions.reason: "Understand" says in plain English what the verb means here (meaning decision m1). Readable names Jesus and says "God the Father" so the reader sees who "the one who sent me" is; the narrator, not the hearers, knows this.

records.source: εἶπεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ὅταν ὑψώσητε τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, τότε γνώσεσθε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι, καὶ ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ ποιῶ οὐδέν, ἀλλὰ καθὼς ἐδίδαξέν με ὁ πατὴρ ταῦτα λαλῶ.
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jesus, "When you lift up the Son of the Man, then you will know that I am, and from myself I do nothing, but just as taught me the Father, these things I speak.

L.28: So Jesus said, "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and [that] I do nothing from {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, but just as the Father taught {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, these things I speak.

R.28: So Jesus said, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am. You will know that I do nothing just on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own. The things I say are what the Father taught {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: lift up: raise on the cross, and by that exalt
decisions.reason: The verb means both to raise something high and to exalt someone. John says it points to the way Jesus would die (12:32-33), and 3:14 and 12:34 use it the same way. In the Greek of Isaiah 52:13 the LORD's servant "will be lifted up and glorified". The cross is where he is raised up and where he is glorified, so every level keeps "lift up" with both senses.

decisions.choice: you will lift him up: his hearers will put him to death, and his death will show who he is
decisions.reason: Jesus says that they will do the lifting up: those who seek to kill him (8:37, 40) will hand him over to be crucified (19:15-16). His death will not be his defeat but the moment that reveals him. "Then you will know" may mean that some will come to see the truth after the cross, or that they will know it too late, to their judgment; John leaves both open (compare 12:32 and 19:37).

decisions.choice: I am: as in 8:24, the words God uses of himself
alternatives: a plain "I am he": I am the one I claim to be
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m1 at 8:24. "You will know that I am" is close to Isaiah 43:10, "that you may know and believe ... that I am", where God speaks of himself. Here the knowing is tied to the cross, where the Son is glorified (12:23; 17:1). Marked uncertain as at 8:24; the footnote gives "that I am he".

decisions.choice: and that I do nothing on my own: still part of what they will know
alternatives: a separate statement: "And I do nothing on my own ..."
decisions.reason: The "and" most likely continues what they will know: that he is who he says, and that all he does and says comes from the Father. It could also begin a fresh statement; the sense is much the same. The words repeat 5:19, 30 and 7:16-17.

decisions.choice: lift up / lifted up, with no "on the cross"; that I am, with no "he"
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice keeps "lifted up" at every level, as at 3:14; adding "on the cross" would lose the exaltation (meaning decision m1). "That I am" is kept bare at every level, as at 8:24 (rendering decision r-en-1 there).

decisions.choice: on my own (B); just on my own, The things I say are what the Father taught me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "on my own", as at 5:19 and 5:30. Readable breaks the sentence into three and repeats "you will know" so the link is clear (meaning decision m4).

records.source: καὶ ὁ πέμψας με μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἐστιν· οὐκ ἀφῆκέν με μόνον, ὅτι ἐγὼ τὰ ἀρεστὰ αὐτῷ ποιῶ πάντοτε.
records.gloss: And the [one] having sent me with me is; not he left me alone, because I the things pleasing to him do always."

L.29: And the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has not left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} alone, because I do the things pleasing to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} always."

R.29: The one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is here with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. He has not left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own, because I always do what makes {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} glad."

decisions.choice: the one who sent me is with me: the Father's presence with the Son
decisions.reason: The Father who sent him has not sent him off alone: he is with him in all he does. Jesus says the same in 8:16 and again on the night before his death, "I am not alone, for the Father is with me" (16:32).

decisions.choice: has not left me alone: a settled fact
alternatives: did not leave me alone when he sent me
decisions.reason: The past tense looks at the whole of his mission: the Father has never left him on his own. It may look back to the sending itself; the meaning is much the same.

decisions.choice: because I always do what pleases him: the reason, and the sign, of the Father's presence
alternatives: only the evidence that the Father is with him
decisions.reason: The clause gives the reason the Father stays with him, but it also shows it: his perfect obedience is the mark of their unity (4:34; 5:30; 6:38). "Always" stands at the end for emphasis.

decisions.choice: at all times I do what is pleasing to him (B); always do what makes him glad, here with me, on my own (R)
alternatives: I do the things pleasing to him always (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the emphasis on "always" by putting "at all times" first. Readable uses everyday words for "pleasing" and "alone".

records.source: ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτόν.
records.gloss: These things of him speaking, many believed in him.

L.30: While {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking these things, many believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.30: While Jesus was saying these things, many people believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: believed in him: a real but untested belief
decisions.reason: John uses the same words for true faith (3:16) and for belief that does not yet go deep (2:23-25; 7:31). The next verses test it: Jesus speaks to "the Jews who had believed him" (8:31), and by the end of the chapter they want to stone him (8:59). John does not say whether these are exactly the same people.

decisions.choice: while he was saying these things: at the time he spoke
decisions.reason: The construction gives the time and also suggests the cause: it was his words, not a sign, that led them to believe.

decisions.choice: many: from among his hearers
decisions.reason: "Many" is not defined. They come from the people listening in the temple, the same setting in which others mocked him (8:22). John often reports belief and hostility side by side (7:31-32; 10:19-21; 11:45-46).

decisions.choice: many people, came to believe (B); Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "many people"; Balanced says "came to believe" to show that their belief began here. Readable names Jesus at the start of a new paragraph.

records.source: Ἔλεγεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς πρὸς τοὺς πεπιστευκότας αὐτῷ Ἰουδαίους· Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ, ἀληθῶς μαθηταί μού ἐστε, καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: Was saying therefore the Jesus to the [ones] having believed him Jews, "If you remain in the word the my, truly disciples of me you are, \v 32 and you will know the truth, and the truth will free you."

L.31: So Jesus was saying to the Jews who had believed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "If you remain in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word, truly you are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} disciples,
L.32: and you will know the truth, and the truth will free you."

R.31: Jesus spoke to the Jews in the crowd who had believed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He said, "If you remain in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word and live by it, you really are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} disciples.
R.32: You will know the truth, and the truth will free you."

decisions.choice: the Jews: Jewish people in the crowd at the temple in Jerusalem who had just come to believe Jesus
decisions.reason: This occurrence does not mean the authorities, and it does not mean the Jewish people as a whole. John has just said that as Jesus spoke in the temple (8:20) many believed in him (8:30); these are the people he now turns to. They are Jews, as Jesus himself, his disciples and his mother are.

decisions.choice: had believed him: the same believers as in 8:30, though the wording changes
alternatives: the change marks a weaker, merely outward belief
decisions.reason: 8:30 says that many "believed in him"; here John writes "having believed him", the perfect participle with the plain dative. In John the two ways of speaking often overlap (compare 5:24 with 6:29), so the change of wording does not by itself show a weaker belief. What follows does show that this new belief is tested at once: Jesus makes remaining in his word the mark of a true disciple, and the talk turns hard (8:33, 37). Whether John means the change of wording to hint at that is uncertain.

decisions.choice: remain in my word: keep holding to Jesus's message and living by it
decisions.reason: Starting to believe is not yet the whole of discipleship; a true disciple stays with what Jesus says. "Remain" is one of John's key verbs (6:56; 15:4-10), and 8:35 picks it up again: the slave does not remain in the house, the son remains. "Word" is Jesus's message as a whole, which he received from the Father (8:26, 28, 38). "Truly" means really, in fact, as opposed to in name only.

decisions.choice: the truth will free you: the truth that Jesus reveals sets people free from slavery to sin
decisions.reason: Knowing the truth is not learning a fact but coming to know God as Jesus makes him known (1:17-18; 17:3); Jesus himself is the truth (14:6). The freedom is explained in 8:34-36: freedom from slavery to sin, given by the Son. The hearers take it as political or social freedom (8:33).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself and "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: the truth will free you
alternatives: the truth will set you free
the truth will make you free
decisions.reason: The verb is "free", the same word Jesus uses in 8:36 ("if the Son frees you") and the root of "free" in 8:33 and 8:36; the plain verb keeps the three verses visibly linked. "Set you free" or "make you free", the familiar wording, means the same.

decisions.choice: in the crowd; remain in my word and live by it
decisions.reason: Readable says where these Jews were (8:20, 30) and adds "and live by it" to explain what remaining in a word means (meaning decision m3). "Remain" itself is kept, since 8:35 plays on it.

records.heading: The truth will free you

records.source: ἀπεκρίθησαν πρὸς αὐτόν· Σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ ἐσμεν καὶ οὐδενὶ δεδουλεύκαμεν πώποτε· πῶς σὺ λέγεις ὅτι Ἐλεύθεροι γενήσεσθε;
records.gloss: They answered to him, "Seed of Abraham we are, and to no one have we been slaves ever; how do you say that, 'Free you will become'?"

L.33: They answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "We are Abraham's seed, and we have never at any time been slaves to anyone. How [is it that] {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} say, 'You will become free'?"

R.33: They answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "We come from Abraham's family, and we have never been anyone's slaves. What do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} mean when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} say that we will become free?"

decisions.choice: they answered: the hearers of 8:31, with the crowd around them
alternatives: the crowd as a whole, no longer the new believers
decisions.reason: John does not change the subject, so the reply comes from those Jesus has just spoken to, the people who had believed him (8:31). As the talk goes on, Jesus says "you are seeking to kill me" (8:37, 40), which fits those in the temple crowd and among the authorities who were already seeking his death (7:1, 19-20, 25, 30). The text does not say exactly where the line runs between the new believers and the others listening; it is plain only that the replies come from people in that crowd.

decisions.choice: seed of Abraham: Abraham's descendants, heirs of God's promise to him
decisions.reason: "Seed" is the Bible's word for descendants (Genesis 12:7; 15:5; 22:17-18). To be Abraham's seed was to belong to the people God had chosen and promised to bless. Jesus grants that they are (8:37); the question he raises is what kind of children they are (8:39).

decisions.choice: never slaves to anyone: a claim to free standing that their own history did not bear out
decisions.reason: Israel had been slaves in Egypt (Exodus 20:2, "out of the house of slavery"), had been taken into exile in Babylon, and in Jesus's day lived under Roman rule. The hearers most likely mean that as Abraham's descendants they had never been anyone's property, whatever foreign power ruled them. Jesus answers on another level: the slavery he means is slavery to sin (8:34).

decisions.choice: descended from Abraham (B); come from Abraham's family (R)
decisions.reason: "Seed" (Literal) is the Bible's own picture, but in everyday speech it does not mean descendants; Balanced and Readable say it plainly (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: What do you mean ...?
decisions.reason: The question "how do you say" is a protest, not a request for information; Balanced and Readable put it the way English protests. Literal keeps "How [is it that] you say".

decisions.choice: slaves
decisions.reason: "Slaves" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free: the hearers deny ever being slaves in answer to "you will become free" (m3; 8:32-36).

records.source: Ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν δοῦλός ἐστιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας·
records.gloss: Answered them the Jesus, "Truly truly I say to you that everyone the [one] doing the sin a slave is of the sin;

L.34: Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly I say to you, everyone who does sin is a slave of sin.

R.34: Jesus answered, "I tell you the truth: anyone who keeps on sinning is a slave to sin.

decisions.choice: everyone who does sin: a person whose life is given over to sin
alternatives: anyone who commits a single sin
decisions.reason: The present participle with "the sin" describes someone who goes on doing sin, a settled way of living, not a single wrong act. 1 John uses the same phrase (1 John 3:4, 8-9). Jesus is not singling out his hearers here: the saying is about everyone.

decisions.choice: slave: a person owned by a master, with no rights of his own
decisions.reason: δοῦλός is the word for a slave, someone who was another's property and could be bought, sold or sent away (8:35). Here the master is sin itself. Jesus answers their claim never to have been slaves (8:33): the slavery that matters is not to a foreign power but to sin.

decisions.choice: a slave of sin (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Nearly all manuscripts have "of sin". A few witnesses leave it out, among them Codex Bezae and some early versions, which gives "everyone who does sin is a slave" and leads straight into the household picture of 8:35. The sense is the same either way. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery to sin is set against freedom (8:32, 36): Jesus says that such a person is owned. Meaning decision m2 says what a slave's position was.

records.source: ὁ δὲ δοῦλος οὐ μένει ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα· ὁ υἱὸς μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.
records.gloss: The but slave not remains in the house into the age; the son remains into the age.

L.35: And the slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever.

R.35: A slave does not remain in the family's house forever. A slave can be sent away. But a son remains forever.

decisions.choice: a household picture: a slave has no lasting place in the house; a son belongs to it
decisions.reason: In a household of the time a slave belonged to the family as property and could be sold or sent away at the master's will; a son was the heir and belonged there for good. Jesus moves from "slave of sin" (8:34) to this everyday picture: a slave's place is never secure.

decisions.choice: possibly Abraham's own household: Ishmael sent away, Isaac the heir (Genesis 21:10)
decisions.reason: The hearers have just claimed to be Abraham's seed (8:33). In Abraham's house the son of the slave woman was sent away while Isaac remained as heir (Genesis 21:10-12), and Paul draws on the same story (Galatians 4:21-31). John does not name it, so the echo is possible but not certain; the picture makes sense as ordinary household life.

decisions.choice: the son: a general picture that points to Jesus, the Son
alternatives: the Son: Jesus only, not a general picture
decisions.reason: Like "the slave", "the son" is any son of a household. But 8:36 applies it at once to Jesus, the Son who can free slaves; the picture is told with him in view. "Remains" picks up 8:31: the disciple who remains in Jesus's word shares the place of the son.

decisions.choice: son (lowercase)
decisions.reason: In 8:35 "son" is part of the picture of any household, so it is not capitalised; in 8:36 it refers to Jesus and is written "Son" (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: for good (B); forever (L, R)
decisions.reason: "For good" says that the slave's stay is never permanent, which is the point of "into the age" here; Literal and Readable keep "forever". Readable adds "A slave can be sent away", the reason a slave does not remain (meaning decision m1), and "the family's house" for the household.

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free: the slave who can be sent away is set against the son who belongs, and against the Son who sets people free (8:34, 36; m1).

records.source: ἐὰν οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθερώσῃ, ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔσεσθε.
records.gloss: If therefore the son you frees, really free you will be.

L.36: If therefore the Son frees you, you will be really free.

R.36: So if the Son frees you, you will really be free.

decisions.choice: the Son: Jesus, the Son of the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus now applies the picture of 8:35 to himself. Only one who belongs to the house for good can set its slaves free; the Son has that place with the Father (3:35; 5:19-23). In 8:32 the truth frees; here the Son does: Jesus is himself the truth (14:6).

decisions.choice: really free: free in fact, not only in name
decisions.reason: The adverb means "in reality". It answers the hearers' claim that they had never been slaves (8:33): the freedom they claim is outward, while the freedom the Son gives is freedom from slavery to sin (8:34).

decisions.choice: Son (capitalised)
decisions.reason: Here "the son" of 8:35 is Jesus himself, so every level writes "Son". "Frees" is the same verb as in 8:32.

records.source: οἶδα ὅτι σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ ἐστε· ἀλλὰ ζητεῖτέ με ἀποκτεῖναι, ὅτι ὁ λόγος ὁ ἐμὸς οὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: I know that seed of Abraham you are; but you seek me to kill, because the word the my not has room in you.

L.37: I know that you are Abraham's seed; but you seek to kill {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, because {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word has no room in you.

R.37: I know that you come from Abraham's family. But you want to kill {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, because you have no room in you for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word.

decisions.choice: Jesus grants that they are Abraham's descendants
decisions.reason: Jesus does not deny their descent from Abraham. The question he raises in what follows (8:39-44) is not who their ancestors are but whose works they are doing.

decisions.choice: you seek to kill me: said to those in the crowd who were seeking his death
alternatives: every one of the new believers of 8:31 sought his death
decisions.reason: The plural "you" is the people Jesus is speaking with in the temple. The attempt on his life was already under way: the authorities wanted to kill him (5:18; 7:1) and had sent officers to arrest him (7:32), and some of the people of Jerusalem knew it (7:25). The text does not say that every listener, or the new believers of 8:31, shared that aim; it holds that this crowd as a whole was not receiving his word. At the end of the chapter some of them pick up stones (8:59).

decisions.choice: my word has no room in you: you do not make room for my word, so it cannot take hold
alternatives: my word makes no progress among you
decisions.reason: The verb χωρεῖ means to have room, to find a place, or to make headway. Either way the sense is that Jesus's word is not received; that is why they want to be rid of him.

decisions.choice: is making no headway in you (B); you have no room in you for my word (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the picture of progress, Readable that of room; both are senses of the verb (meaning decision m3), and both say the word is not received.

records.source: ἃ ἐγὼ ἑώρακα παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ λαλῶ· καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν ἃ ἠκούσατε παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ποιεῖτε.
records.gloss: What I have seen with the father I speak; and you therefore what you heard from the father you do.

L.38: What I have seen with the Father I speak; and you therefore do what you heard from the father."

R.38: I tell you what I have seen with {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father. And in the same way, you do what you have heard from your father."

decisions.choice: the Father ... the father, without possessives (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts have no possessives. Many later manuscripts read "my Father" in the first half and "your father" in the second, which makes plain that two different fathers are meant. Some also read "what you have seen" for "what you heard". Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: you do: a statement contrasting two fathers, the father named in 8:44
alternatives: a command: so you too must do what you heard from the Father
decisions.reason: The verb can be a statement ("you do") or a command ("so you too must do"). Read as a command, both fathers are God, and Jesus urges them to do what they have heard from the Father. Read as a statement, as here, Jesus contrasts his Father with theirs, whom he names in 8:44; the next verses support this, since they protest that their father is Abraham (8:39) and Jesus answers that they do the works of their father (8:41). The difference matters, and the evidence is not decisive.

decisions.choice: what I have seen with the Father: Jesus speaks from his own presence with God
decisions.reason: Jesus has been with the Father and speaks what he has seen and heard there (1:18; 3:11, 32; 8:26, 28). The hearers, by contrast, act on what they "heard" from another source.

decisions.choice: the Father (capitalised) ... the father (lowercase)
alternatives: the Father in both places (if the verb is a command)
decisions.reason: Capital letters are a choice the Greek does not make. Following meaning decision m2, the first father is God and is capitalised; the second is the other father of 8:44 and is not. Readable supplies "my" and "your", as many manuscripts have them (meaning decision m1).

records.source: Ἀπεκρίθησαν καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ ἐστιν.
records.gloss: They answered and said to him, "The father of us Abraham is."

L.39: They answered and said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Our father is Abraham."

decisions.choice: our father is Abraham: they rest their standing on their descent
decisions.reason: Israel looked to Abraham as its father (Isaiah 51:2), and to be his descendants was to share God's promise to him. John the Baptist had warned against trusting in that alone (Matthew 3:9). The hearers have sensed that Jesus means a different father (8:38) and answer by naming Abraham.

decisions.choice: They replied (B); They answered (R)
decisions.reason: "Answered and said" is a Hebrew way of introducing a reply; Literal keeps both verbs, Balanced and Readable use one.

records.source: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Εἰ τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ ἐστε, τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἐποιεῖτε·
records.gloss: Says to them the Jesus, "If children of the Abraham you are, the works of the Abraham you would be doing;

L.39: Jesus says to them, "If you are children of Abraham, you would be doing the works of Abraham.

R.39: Jesus said to them, "If you really are Abraham's children, you would be doing the things Abraham did.

decisions.choice: if you are ... you would be doing (SBLGNT)
alternatives: if you were Abraham's children, you would be doing
if you are Abraham's children, do the works of Abraham
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ in both verbs. The SBLGNT reads "if you are ... you would be doing", a mixed form that implies they are not doing Abraham's works. Some manuscripts read "if you were ... you would be doing", a plain condition contrary to fact; others read "if you are ... do the works of Abraham", a command. All three say that Abraham's true children act like him. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: children of Abraham: those who share Abraham's character, not only his descent
decisions.reason: Jesus has granted that they are Abraham's seed (8:37); now he speaks of being his children, which in the Bible's way of speaking means resembling a father in what one does. The same thought is in 8:41 and 8:44, and Paul speaks of Abraham's children in a similar way (Romans 4:11-12; Galatians 3:7).

decisions.choice: the works of Abraham: Abraham believed God and welcomed those God sent
decisions.reason: Abraham trusted and obeyed God's word (Genesis 12:1-4; 15:6; 22:1-18) and received God's messengers with hospitality (Genesis 18:1-8). 8:40 makes the contrast: they seek to kill one who brings them the truth from God.

decisions.choice: said (B, R); says (Literal)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("says"). Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English narrative does. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: If you really are
decisions.reason: Readable adds "really" to bring out the challenge in the mixed condition (meaning decision m1): Jesus doubts that they are Abraham's children in the full sense.

records.source: νῦν δὲ ζητεῖτέ με ἀποκτεῖναι, ἄνθρωπον ὃς τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὑμῖν λελάληκα ἣν ἤκουσα παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ· τοῦτο Ἀβραὰμ οὐκ ἐποίησεν.
records.gloss: Now but you seek me to kill, a man who the truth to you has spoken which I heard from the God; this Abraham not did.

L.40: But now you seek to kill {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God. This Abraham did not do.

R.40: But now you want to kill {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. I am a man who has told you the truth I heard from God. Abraham never did anything like this.

decisions.choice: but now: as things actually stand
decisions.reason: "Now" here is not mainly about time; it sets what they are doing against what Abraham's children would do (8:39).

decisions.choice: a man: a human being
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of himself as a man who has brought them the truth he heard from God. The word stresses that he stands before them as a human messenger; the same word is used by others of him (4:29; 9:11; 19:5).

decisions.choice: this Abraham did not do: Abraham did not reject God's messenger
decisions.reason: Abraham welcomed those whom God sent (Genesis 18:1-8) and believed God's word (Genesis 15:6). Seeking to kill one who speaks God's truth is the opposite of Abraham's works.

decisions.choice: three short sentences
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the sentence up and turns "a man who" into "I am a man who".

records.source: ὑμεῖς ποιεῖτε τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: You do the works of the father of you."

L.41: You do the works of your father."

R.41: You are doing the things your own father does."

decisions.choice: your father: a father other than Abraham, not yet named
decisions.reason: Jesus judges by works, as in 8:39: a child shows his father by what he does. He does not yet say who this father is; he names him in 8:44. The works in view are the ones just named: seeking to kill a man who speaks the truth (8:37, 40).

decisions.choice: your own father
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "own" to bring out the emphatic "you" and the contrast with Abraham in 8:40.

records.source: εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Ἡμεῖς ἐκ πορνείας οὐ γεγεννήμεθα· ἕνα πατέρα ἔχομεν τὸν θεόν.
records.gloss: They said to him, "We of sexual immorality not have been born; one father we have, the God."

L.41: They said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "We were not born of sexual immorality; one Father we have: God."

R.41: They said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "We were not born from sexual sin. We have only one Father, and that is God."

decisions.choice: not born of sexual immorality: they deny being unfaithful to God, perhaps with a jab at Jesus's birth
alternatives: a plain claim about their own birth and descent
chiefly an insult about Jesus's birth
decisions.reason: The prophets call Israel's turning to other gods sexual unfaithfulness, and its people "children of whoredom" (Hosea 1:2; 2:4). The hearers answer that they are no such children: they worship the one God and he alone is their Father (Malachi 2:10). The emphatic "we" may also hint "unlike you": Jesus's mother was found to be with child before her marriage (Matthew 1:18-19), and the hearers will go on to insult him (8:48). The text does not make that hint explicit, so it remains a possibility.

decisions.choice: one Father, God: they claim God himself as their Father
decisions.reason: God is called Israel's Father in Scripture (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; 64:8). Having been told that their deeds do not match Abraham, they reach past him to God. Jesus answers that claim in 8:42.

decisions.choice: sexual immorality (L); sexual sin (B, R)
decisions.reason: The word covers every kind of sexual sin, including prostitution, and the prophets use it for idolatry (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable use the plainer phrase; "illegitimate" would decide for one reading of the sentence.

records.source: εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Εἰ ὁ θεὸς πατὴρ ὑμῶν ἦν ἠγαπᾶτε ἂν ἐμέ, ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐξῆλθον καὶ ἥκω· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ ἐλήλυθα, ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνός με ἀπέστειλεν.
records.gloss: Said to them the Jesus, "If the God father of you were, you would love me, I for from the God came out and am here; not even for from myself have I come, but that one me sent.

L.42: Jesus said to them, "If God were your Father, you would love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, for I came out from God and am here; for I have not come of {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.42: Jesus said to them, "If God really were your Father, you would love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. I came from God, and now I am here. I did not come on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own. God sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: if God were your Father, you would love me: implying that, in this sense, he is not
decisions.reason: The form of the sentence is contrary to fact. A true child of God would recognise and love the one who comes from God (compare 5:42-43; 1 John 5:1). Jesus judges the claim of 8:41 by the same test of family likeness as in 8:39.

decisions.choice: I came out from God and am here: Jesus's origin with God and his coming into the world
decisions.reason: "Came out from God" speaks of where he comes from (13:3; 16:27-28); "am here" says that he has arrived and is present among them.

decisions.choice: not of myself, but he sent me: Jesus comes as the Father's envoy
decisions.reason: Jesus did not come on his own initiative or authority (5:30; 7:28-29). The one who sent him is God, the Father he has just spoken of; "that one" is how John often refers to God or to Jesus.

decisions.choice: God sent me
decisions.reason: Readable names God where the Greek says "that one", and adds "really" in the first line to bring out the contrary-to-fact form (meaning decision m1).

records.source: διὰ τί τὴν λαλιὰν τὴν ἐμὴν οὐ γινώσκετε;
records.gloss: Why the speech the my not do you understand?

L.43: Why do you not understand {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} speech?

R.43: Why do you not understand what I am telling you?

decisions.choice: speech: the way Jesus talks, as distinct from his word
alternatives: my word (the same as in the next sentence)
decisions.reason: λαλιὰν means talk or way of speaking; in the next sentence Jesus uses λόγον, "word", for his message. They do not follow what he says on the surface because they cannot accept the message behind it.

decisions.choice: what I am saying (B); what I am telling you (R)
decisions.reason: "Speech" (Literal) keeps a separate word from "word" in the next sentence; Balanced and Readable use the everyday phrase for what someone is saying.

records.source: ὅτι οὐ δύνασθε ἀκούειν τὸν λόγον τὸν ἐμόν.
records.gloss: Because not you are able to hear the word the my.

L.43: Because you are not able to hear {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word.

R.43: It is because you cannot stand to hear {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word.

decisions.choice: cannot hear: cannot bring themselves to listen and accept
decisions.reason: "Hear" in Scripture often means to listen and obey (Deuteronomy 6:4). They hear the sounds, but they cannot accept the message. In John, such inability goes with an unwillingness of the heart (5:40, 44; 12:39-40), as 8:44 says: they want to do another's desires.

decisions.choice: cannot bear to listen (B); cannot stand to hear (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "bear" or "stand" so that "cannot hear" is not taken as a matter of the ears (meaning decision m1). "It is because" makes the answer a full sentence.

records.source: ὑμεῖς ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς τοῦ διαβόλου ἐστὲ καὶ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν θέλετε ποιεῖν.
records.gloss: You of the father the devil are, and the desires of the father of you you want to do.

L.44: You are of [your] father the devil, and the desires of your father you want to do.

R.44: Your father is the devil, and you want to do what your father wants.

decisions.choice: said to these hearers who are seeking to kill him: it names whose works they are doing, not their descent or their people
alternatives: a statement about the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Jesus has granted that they are Abraham's descendants (8:37), and he has been judging fatherhood by works throughout (8:39, 41). The works in question are seeking to kill a man who speaks the truth (8:37, 40), and murder and lying are what this verse goes on to say are the devil's own works. So the charge is about what these particular hearers are doing to Jesus, not about who their ancestors are and not about a people. The same language is used of anyone who does such deeds: 1 John 3:8-12 says that whoever does sin is "of the devil" and gives Cain as the example; Jesus calls Peter "Satan" (Matthew 16:23) and says that one of the Twelve is a devil (6:70). The text does not say that the Jewish people are children of the devil: Jesus, his disciples and his mother are Jews, and many in this same crowd had just believed him (8:30).

decisions.choice: of the father, the devil: the devil is the father, not the father of the devil
alternatives: of the father of the devil
decisions.reason: The two nouns stand side by side, "the father, the devil", and the second names the first. The words could be read as "of the father of the devil", but nothing in John speaks of such a figure, and the rest of the verse describes the devil himself as the father.

decisions.choice: you want to do his desires: they choose what he wants
decisions.reason: "Want" is the verb of will and choice. They are not helpless; they are willing to carry out what the devil desires, and the next sentence says what that is: killing and lying.

decisions.choice: Your father is the devil
alternatives: You belong to your father, the devil
You are of your father the devil (Literal)
decisions.reason: "You are of your father" means "you come from your father"; Balanced and Readable say it in plain English without changing the force of the charge. Balanced uses "choose" for the verb of will (meaning decision m3).

records.source: ἐκεῖνος ἀνθρωποκτόνος ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ οὐκ ἔστηκεν, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἀλήθεια ἐν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: That one a murderer was from beginning, and in the truth not stood, because not is truth in him.

L.44: That one was a murderer from [the] beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him.

R.44: He was a murderer from the very beginning. He has never kept to the truth, because there is no truth in him.

decisions.choice: a murderer from the beginning: the devil brought death into the world (Genesis 3), and his work showed in Cain (Genesis 4:8)
decisions.reason: In Genesis 3 the serpent's lie led to human death (Genesis 2:17; 3:4, 19); in Genesis 4:8 Cain killed his brother, and 1 John 3:12 says Cain "was of the evil one". Either or both may be in view. The word means a killer of human beings, and it ties back to 8:37 and 8:40: those who seek to kill Jesus are doing the devil's work.

decisions.choice: did not stand in the truth: he never held his ground in it
alternatives: he does not stand in the truth
decisions.reason: The source data parses ἔστηκεν as an imperfect: he did not stand, or was not standing, in the truth. Early manuscripts have no accents or breathings, and with a different breathing the same letters are a perfect, "he does not stand". Either way the devil has no footing in the truth, and the reason follows: there is no truth in him.

decisions.choice: has never kept to the truth
decisions.reason: Readable puts "not stand in the truth" in plain words.

records.source: ὅταν λαλῇ τὸ ψεῦδος, ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων λαλεῖ, ὅτι ψεύστης ἐστὶν καὶ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: When he speaks the lie, from the own [things] he speaks, because a liar he is and the father of it.

L.44: Whenever he speaks the lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and the father of it.

R.44: When he lies, he is speaking from what he really is. He is a liar, and the father of lies.

decisions.choice: the father of it: the father of lying, the one from whom falsehood comes
alternatives: he is a liar, and so is his father
decisions.reason: "Of it" (αὐτοῦ) may point back to "the lie" (falsehood itself) or to "liar" (the father of every liar). Both say that lying starts with him. The words can also be read "he is a liar, and so is his father", but that would give the devil a father, which nothing in Scripture suggests.

decisions.choice: he speaks from his own: lying is his own nature
decisions.reason: Jesus says that he does not speak from himself but what the Father gives him (7:16-18; 8:28; 12:49). The devil is the opposite: when he lies, he is speaking out of what belongs to him.

decisions.choice: the lie: possibly the serpent's first lie (Genesis 3:4)
decisions.reason: The article may simply mark lying in general, or it may recall the lie of Genesis 3:4, "You will not surely die", which goes with "murderer from the beginning".

decisions.choice: the father of lies
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "of it" refers to (meaning decision m1). Readable says "from what he really is" for "from his own".

records.source: ἐγὼ δὲ ὅτι τὴν ἀλήθειαν λέγω, οὐ πιστεύετέ μοι.
records.gloss: I but because the truth I speak, not you believe me.

L.45: But I, because I speak the truth, you do not believe {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.45: But I tell you the truth, and that is why you do not believe {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: but I ... because: Jesus sets himself against the liar, and the truth is the reason they do not believe
decisions.reason: The emphatic "I" contrasts Jesus with the devil of 8:44. One would expect "although I speak the truth"; Jesus says "because": since they belong to the father of lies, the truth itself is what they reject.

decisions.choice: But as for me, it is because ... (B); and that is why (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek begins with "I" and then changes course. Balanced keeps the stress on "me" with "as for me"; Readable makes two clauses. Literal keeps the broken sentence.

records.source: τίς ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐλέγχει με περὶ ἁμαρτίας;
records.gloss: Who of you convicts me concerning sin?

L.46: Who of you convicts {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} of sin?

R.46: Can any one of you show that I have ever sinned?

decisions.choice: convicts: proves someone guilty
decisions.reason: The verb means to expose or prove guilty, as in a court (16:8). Jesus invites them to bring any charge of wrongdoing against him; under the Law a charge had to be proved (Deuteronomy 19:15).

decisions.choice: sin: wrongdoing of any kind, including speaking falsely
decisions.reason: In this context of truth and lies the word may point especially to falsehood, but it keeps its full sense. It ties back to 8:34: everyone who does sin is its slave, and they cannot show that he is.

decisions.choice: Which of you can prove that I have sinned? (B); Can any one of you show ... (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the challenge as English asks it, with "can"; it is a challenge, not a request for a name.

records.source: εἰ ἀλήθειαν λέγω, διὰ τί ὑμεῖς οὐ πιστεύετέ μοι;
records.gloss: If truth I speak, why you not believe me?
